speaker: edwards
text: All right, it's nine o'clock. Welcome to another session, another virtual session of oral arguments from the Fifth District Court of Appeal. We have a split session today, this morning, on the first case, which is 18-34-57, Niven Sumar versus State of Florida. You have me, Judge Edwards, you have Judge Lambert and Judge Harris. For the thousands of viewers on YouTube, there's another session starting at 10 o'clock, and there are cases at 10 and 11 with a different panel. We will go ahead and start here in just a minute. You can see the clock in the one panel there. It's the same clock you've been using. If you want anything other than five minutes for rebuttal, Mr. Pinal, please let us know, and our marshal will set it accordingly. And as usual, when the yellow comes on, you're into your rebuttal time. Go ahead, Mr. Pinal, when you're ready.

speaker: williamponall
text: Good morning, may it please the court. My name is William Pinal, and I represent Niven Sumar, the appellant in this case. Please reserve five minutes of my time for rebuttal. Initially, it's our position that the trial court erred by denying Mr. Sumar's motion for judgment of acquittal on all seven counts of the information, because the state failed to prove that he was the person that set the fire or that he acted as a principal in this case. We anticipate that the state is gonna argue that the special standard of review for circumstantial evidence cases no longer applies based on the Supreme Court's decision in Bush, and we disagree with that for several reasons. But even if that standard does apply to this case, we believe a judgment of acquittal was still required. It's our position that Bush does not apply because it was not the law at the time of the trial in this case. Both co-defendants tailored their strategies to the law at the time of the trial. They argued the circumstantial evidence standard at the time of J-O-A, at the end of the defense case, and at the end of the state case. The trial court applied that standard to grant a judgment of acquittal for Mr. Sumar's father, Serge Sumar, and applied that same standard to deny Niven Sumar's J-O-A. So it's our position at this court to be determining whether the trial court made a mistake or erred under the standard at the time of the trial, not a standard that was announced over a year after the trial by the Florida Supreme Court. In support of that position, we cite the Morales case, which we filed a supplemental authority last week. In that case, while the case was on appeal, it was an entrapment case. While the case was on appeal, the Florida Supreme Court added an element to the defense of entrapment. And what the court said was that, based on the law in effect at the time of Morales' trial, neither the state nor the defense could have anticipated the need to satisfy the evidential requirements of Nunez. So it's our position, we're in the same situation here.

speaker: elizabethsianoharris
text: That's a little bit different, isn't it? I mean, that one dealt with an element of the crime that the parties didn't know of at the time of the trial. But Bush deals with reviewing the evidence that was presented at trial, I mean, the standard of appellate review. How is that analogous to the case you cited in your supplemental authority?

speaker: williamponall
text: Sure, I respectfully disagree. It is a standard of appellate review, but it's also the standard the trial judge uses to determine whether JOA should be granted at the time of trial. Certainly, the defendants in this case were aware of the case law and cited the case law circumstantial evidence to the trial judge and may have made decisions based on what witnesses to present at the time of trial. For instance, Naveen Sumar did not choose to testify in this case. Had the standard been different, that he may have made a different decision. I mean, the whole standard and process and reviewing whether a JOA should be granted, the whole standard was changed after trial. So I think it's certainly fair to conclude that the strategy used by the defendants may have been different had they been aware of that.

speaker: edwards
text: And that's what- Even if you applied the laws that was, what's your best case that Mr. Sumar should have gotten off for insufficient evidence?

speaker: williamponall
text: Your best case is the Perez case from the second DCA 2013. The defendant in that case was convicted of arson and burning to defraud and insure. Just like Mr. Sumar, the court noted that-

speaker: edwards
text: The conviction was the same, but the facts were quite different. I mean, there, Mr. Perez claimed he was cooking breakfast and left. The fire marshal or the detective investigating it agreed that the fire did come from the stove. Perez testified without contradiction that when he arrived back home from being somewhere watching a movie with a buddy or a relative, he saw smoke. He went and got a hose, came in, tried to put out the fire. When that didn't work, he asked his neighbor to call 911. I mean, here, the evidence is your client just happened to swing by 436 and Colonial to check out his business on his way from Kissimmee to Tampa, which makes no sense. He lied to the investigator, which again, as the investigator told him, that made him look pretty bad. But here, Mr. Perez had no real motive to set a fire, unlike your client, whose business was failing. He was personally on the lease. He was the contact for the insured and so on and so forth. So, you know, yeah, the convictions were the same, but the evidence was quite different. Don't you agree?

speaker: williamponall
text: I mean, I think the factual circumstances are different, but I think the important facts are similar. Let me start at the end first. The defendant's attorney from the second DCA indicated that even if the defendant had motive and opportunity, that was insufficient to establish sufficient circumstantial evidence to justify a conviction. But back to the-

speaker: edwards
text: Overly, the apartment in Moberly, the girlfriend or the victim's apartment was left open for 30 minutes. Here, the evidence is all the doors were locked. The windows had burglar bars. The fence even around the place was locked. And if you look at what Sumir testified, well, he didn't testify, but in his statements, he said they went by at 5.30. The fire started at like 5.34 based on the burglar alarms. So if your hypothesis of innocence is that Jose Feliciano or Brian, the salesman came by, you know, nobody saw a car, no evidence of that. So within a couple of minutes of when he swung by, they snuck in there real quick, started the fire and got out. I mean, that's quite different than Mobley where it was definitely open for 30 minutes.

speaker: williamponall
text: Well, Judge, for all we know, Mr. Feliciano or Mr. Nelson could have been inside the building before when they swung by. So I hear what you're saying, but I think we're limiting the facts a little bit too much. What the important of Perez and Mobley is, is that simply being present at the scene doesn't establish that you started the fire. And there really is no evidence and a stake in seeds. They can't say whether, they cannot establish who started the fire in this case. And they introduced no evidence suggesting that either Mr. Shumar or his father started the fire or took any actions in support of starting the fire. What the Perez case pointed out is very important was that no one in that case took samples from the clothing or person on the day of the fire to determine whether they had been in contact with gasoline or some other accelerants.

speaker: edwards
text: Did Mr. Shumar change clothes after he took a shower?

speaker: williamponall
text: I'm not sure that's the case or not, but certainly no one sought to get the clothes or test him to see whether he'd been in contact with an accelerant. So this isn't a situation where you have evidence that he was involved with fire or they found an accelerant in his possession or like the Bush case where they found evidence of fingerprints on the murder weapon. All you have is evidence that he was near the scene at the time the fire started or shortly before the time that the fire started.

speaker: edwards
text: You actually have evidence from the father's statement that Naveen got out of the car. Father sometimes is asleep, but other times he seems to be awake. It's a little incredible, but if you take his testimony, which you must in a JOA motion, you take his testimony in favor of the state, your client got out of the car. He didn't just drive by, he got out of the car at their shop.

speaker: williamponall
text: But that's entirely consistent with his testimony or statements that he was just checking on the building and checking on the cars outside the building. But he denied getting out of the car, didn't he? But I think initially, and then I think he told the investigator later, he did get out of the car. So, but again, there's still no evidence that he started the fire or did anything to assist in starting the fire. And the state did not eliminate the hypothesis that someone else, including Jose Feliciani, started the fire. In fact, despite the state's argument to the contrary, he never provided that testimony. No one ever asked him whether he started the fire in this case.

speaker: edwards
text: Well, he did say he learned of it from his friend Hector at Napa or whatever the auto parts store. That's what he said he learned of. And once he got that phone call, he did efforts consistent with somebody who didn't start the fire, such as trying to contact your client, the father, and then he came to the fire scene. Kind of the same thing with Brian. Once Brian learned of it, he did things to try to notify your client and came to the fire scene. And both of them got there quicker than either of the Samir.

speaker: williamponall
text: I understand. So it's also consistent with someone trying to, Mr. Feliciani, trying to cover up his earlier actions. Again, they never asked him explicitly, did you start the fire? So it's our position that they did not exclude the reasonable hypothesis that either Mr. Feliciani or some other individual may have started the fire because there was no direct or circumstantial evidence establishing that Mr. Samir started the fire or helped start the fire in this case. So it's our position that Perez and Moberly required the court to grant a judgment of acquittal in this case because there really wasn't any material difference in the positions of Naveen and Serge before the trial court.

speaker: edwards
text: It wasn't exactly the same. There were important differences. Your client was on the lease. Your client was a day-to-day manager. So he knew what the financial status of the business was, which was a 59% decrease over time. He was the one who obtained the insurance policy that was due to expire in a week or two. And he was the one who helped fill out the insurance papers. He drove, he was not asleep, and he got out of the car. So, I mean, you have quite a few differences. I'm not asking you to agree that that's enough, but it's not like the both of them did exactly the same thing and had the same knowledge. There are differences.

speaker: williamponall
text: Certainly there are factual differences. I think the legal implication of those factual differences are actually zero. Mowberley, again, stands for the proposition that just because you have a motive doesn't establish, doesn't make the evidence sufficient. The cases are clear just because you drove to the scene doesn't make you guilty as a principle. That's established in the Taylor case and a robbery where the facts show that Taylor was present at the scene of the robbery and the driver of the car when it left the scene. And they found that the evidence that is not established individually or collectively that he was a principle to robber. So it's our position that, yeah, it looks suspicious, but that's not the standard. The standard is, did they exclude every reasonable hypothesis of innocence? And it's our position that did not do so like they did not for the father in this case. Additionally, in closing argument, the state made a gross misstatement of law indicating that simply Mr. Sumair's family to answer the phone calls from the alarm company on its own was sufficient to constitute the overacting support of being a principle. That's a misstatement of law. And when we're dealing with a case like this, which is based on circumstantial evidence and which is a close case in which a JOA was granted on a co-defendant, there's a strong possibility that that misstatement of law contributed to the guilty verdict in this case. So if the court does not grant a judgment of acquittal, we'd ask that a new trial be granted based on this improper closing argument. And I'd reserve the rest of my time for rebuttal.

speaker: edwards
text: All right, thank you very much. And Ms. Davenport, when you're ready.

speaker: krisdavenport
text: May it please the court. My name is Chris Davenport. I represent the state of Florida in this case. The standard is not whether there's a reasonable hypothesis of innocence. The standard is whether the state presented competent substantial evidence to support the verdict. The Supreme Court made it clear in Bush at page 201 of that opinion. It says this standard should now be used in all cases where the sufficiency of the evidence is analyzed. This is a case where the sufficiency of the evidence is analyzed. I did not know that Mr. Pinnell was gonna take this position that Bush did not apply here because the cases in the pipeline, that's generally how new case law applies to cases in the pipeline. There are other district courts that have addressed this and have found that Bush does apply to pipeline cases. So I will supplement with those today.

speaker: elizabethsianoharris
text: Ms. Davenport, what about Mr. Pinnell's argument that it's the case law that applied at the time the judge denied the JOA and that was pre-Bush? Was that an error or did it be reconsidered then?

speaker: krisdavenport
text: No, well, first of all, it's in theory, an easier standard for the defendant to meet and the trial court still denied it. But at trial, they're arguing to the fact finder, which is the jury and the jury isn't given a special instruction that this is how you should evaluate the evidence, which is why this court's opinion in Knight and ultimately the opinion in Bush got rid of that standard because it doesn't make any sense for the jury to be told, here's what your burden of proof is and then for the trial court and the appellate court to evaluate it differently, that makes no sense at all, which is why Bush got rid of this standard. It's an outlier as they explained very well in that opinion but the easier standard, he couldn't meet that either. It's not like they put on different proof to meet that standard. It's not like there's a different element. It's just a standard of review and they're trying to convince the jury, not the judge and the jury isn't given that special standard. It's long been the law in Florida that if a new case comes out, it applies to all the appellate court cases that are in the pipeline, that are pending on direct appeal when the case comes out and that's what we have here. I think Bush has made it clear that it applies to all cases from the time they issued the opinion, this standard should now be used in all cases. I don't know how you get any clearer than that and like I said, I would be happy to supplement with other district court opinions that apply Bush to these cases that are pending on direct appeal and there are none that don't because this is how it works. This is how it's always worked. Be that as it may, even if this court uses the old overruled night standard, we still have sufficient evidence. His hypothesis of innocence was that somebody else set the fire. Clearly they had to have had a key because the fire department said they had to break in there. They could not get in. Four people had a key, the defendant, the co-defendant and then the two employees. One employee, Mr. Nelson specifically said, I did not start the fire. The other employee said, I left on Friday. The next, I planned to come back on Monday and the next thing I heard was the building was on fire. The jury got to see those witnesses. The jury got to evaluate whether or not they were involved. That was one of the potential hypotheses they threw out in closing argument. The jury obviously didn't buy it. The trial court didn't buy it. That's evidence that conflicts with that reasonable hypothesis. So there is sufficient evidence under either standard, but Bush is a standard that applies here. I believe Judge Edwards has set out in detail the differences between the evidence against the father and the evidence against this defendant. They're in different financial positions as far as knowledge of what was happening in the business. The defendant got out of the car, according to his father. The father said, I was sleeping. So there's more involvement at the scene and certainly more motive for this defendant than anything we had with the father. As far as closing argument went, yes, there's a long analogy made by the prosecutor in his rebuttal closing argument. He was talking about, there's two elements to principles. You have to have the conscious intent that the crime be committed, and then you have to assist or encourage in some way. His argument was focusing on what assistance means. And he was basically saying you didn't have to set the fire. The fact that he was aware of it and did not answer the phone calls was enough to show assistance. He was focusing on that element. He never really talked about the conscious intent element in his analogy. That's obviously a great failure in that analogy, but the jury was told repeatedly by the parties and more importantly by the court that there's two elements to principle. So considering the complete lack of an objection from defense counsel here, we would submit that the defendant has not shown fundamental error. That is the jury could not have reached this verdict without the assistance of this error. These were long closing arguments with a lot of hypotheticals thrown out there. So the fact that he didn't focus on both elements, we would submit is not fundamentally erroneous. So unless the court has questions, we would ask you to affirm the convictions in this case. Thank you.

speaker: edwards
text: Thank you, Mr. Pinnell for your rebuttal.

speaker: williamponall
text: Thank you, Judge. Initially, yeah, we agree that the general rule is if it's in the pipeline, it applies. We think this is unique because we have a change in the law that would have affected the strategy of trial. And it also results in two different standards being applied to co-defendants. And the two cases we filed last week as supplemental authority, Johnson and Lawyer, indicate that that can result in a manifest injustice when similarly situated co-defendants are treated differently. It's undisputed that if we apply the Bush standard here today, that the two co-defendants are getting judged under two different standards. And we think that's inappropriate under the case law. So acknowledging the general pipeline rule, which the state is correct about, we think this is unique because of the procedural posture and because there was co-defendants involved. Additionally, even if the Bush standard applies, we believe the state's evidence was insufficient. Certainly under that standard, all reasonable inferences are resolved in favor of the state. It's our position that just because Mr. Sumir was at the scene and did some suspicious things after the fact, that does not allow a reasonable inference that he started the fire or helped someone start the fire. If that's the appropriate conclusion, then the mere fact that myself or someone else was at their own home shortly before a fire started and gave some questionable statements after the fact would be sufficient to support a conviction for arson. And I don't believe that's the law. And I don't think that's a reasonable inference under the facts of this case or any other case with similar facts. So we believe under either standard that a judgment of acquittal would have been required, but we do believe that the circumstantial evidence standard should be applied in this case because Bush and the other cases that Ms. Davenport refers to from the other DCAs, none of those cases involve co-defendants where two different standards would be applied to the different co-defendants. With regard to the closing argument, an objection from Mr. Naveen Sumir would have been futile as the co-counsel had already overruled it when there was an objection based on misstatement of the law. So it would have been a futile objection to make. So it's our position that it did not need to be made a second time. And the fact that a proper instruction was given to the jury is also not dispositive. All the cases where reversal is found appropriate by the district courts, proper instructions were given. The standard is whether it has the possibility or the probability of misleading the jury, especially in a closed case, which we believe this is, one of the co-defendants was granted JOA. There was no direct or circumstantial evidence showing that Mr. Sumir actually started the fire or did anything to help start the fire. So this is a closed case and the state is arguing to the jury and the state in this case is in rebuttal gets the last word, is telling him, just because they didn't answer the phone, that's sufficient on its own to find the act assisting in the arson.

speaker: edwards
text: Do you consider whether that's reasonable to believe that that possibly is why the jury convicted him simply because he didn't answer his phone?

speaker: williamponall
text: I think with the force and the length of the state's argument and the fact that it's the last argument made to the jury, I think it's reasonable to believe that.

speaker: edwards
text: I think- We should ignore all the other evidence that was presented and just look at the fact that the state's attorney argued that one thing that was certainly not the most accurate statement of the law.

speaker: williamponall
text: Well, I mean, I think that there has to be consequences for gross misstatements of the law. If the evidence is so strong, then they'll have no problem convicting him on retrial. The idea that it's okay and that the appellate court should weigh the evidence, I think is inappropriate. I think the question is, was it an improper argument? I think the state's conceded that. It goes to the essential argument on principles. It's a central disputed issue at trial. So I don't think this court should reweigh the evidence on its own and speculate that the jury would ignore this improper argument. An important argument, it's a misstatement. It's a gross misstatement and it's the last thing the jury heard. So I do believe that the court should grant a new trial on this particular argument if the court's not convinced that a JOA is appropriate. We'd ask that you reverse, thank you.

speaker: edwards
text: All right, thank you very much. We'll be in recess. Thank you.
